title: St Joseph (19 March)
hook: the quiet carpenter, patron of workers and fathers

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Patrick: a kidnapped boy who went back, and a prayer that fills every direction. Your line was christ beside me. Where did you notice it? Day one thousand twenty-four.

Go through the Gospels looking for a single sentence spoken by Joseph, the husband of Mary. You'll come up empty. He has dreams. He gets up in the night. He takes a pregnant fiancée into his home, walks a family to Egypt and back, searches the city for a missing twelve-year-old. And the text never once records him saying a word. Mary speaks. Simeon speaks. Angels speak. Joseph acts. Then, after the stories of Jesus's childhood, he never appears in a scene again. Churches still give him a feast day, and some honor him as the patron of workers and fathers. A whole saint's day for a man who never speaks. Today, St Joseph.
screen: `HE DREAMS. HE GETS UP. HE GOES.`

segments.voice: Matthew's story of Joseph opens at a painful moment. Mary, the woman he's promised to, is pregnant, and not by him. The King James Bible says: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." That comes first. Before any angel, his first instinct is to protect her from shame. He could have made it public, and he chooses to do it quietly. Then the angel comes in a dream and tells him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife. And here is all Matthew gives us of his response: "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife." No speech. No argument. He wakes up and does it. The pattern repeats. Another dream: take the child and flee. Matthew says he arose and took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt. Up in the dark, packing, gone. Later, when the danger is over, the same again, home. Then there's his work. In his home town, people later ask about Jesus, "Is not this the carpenter's son?" The Greek word behind carpenter means a builder or craftsman, someone who works with his hands. Mark's Gospel calls Jesus himself the carpenter, so tradition pictures him learning the trade from this quiet man. That's why Catholics in particular honor Joseph as patron of workers and of fathers, and of families. Some Orthodox and Protestant Christians honor him too, as the righteous man who sheltered the holy family. Across these traditions, the picture is of faith that shows up mostly as getting up and doing the next thing.
screen: `A JUST MAN, MINDED TO SPARE HER SHAME.`
`RAISED FROM SLEEP, HE DID AS BIDDEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a father figure in your life. Your own father, if that's a good place to go, or a grandfather, an uncle, a coach, a teacher, an older neighbor who once fixed your bike and asked nothing for it. Someone who mostly showed up rather than talked. Settle, and breathe. Let one specific thing they did come back to you, as clearly as you can. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, simply hold the memory with gratitude. Then decide how you'll thank them, or honor them if they're gone. The bell holds the time.
St Joseph. The husband of Mary and the carpenter of Nazareth, who in the Gospels never speaks, and keeps getting up to do what he was asked.
Your line: the quiet one. Today, send a short thank-you to someone who looked after you without fuss, and name the thing they did. Day one thousand twenty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the solemnity of St Joseph in March, and in parts of Italy and among Italian-American families, St Joseph's tables of food are set out and shared with the poor; Anglicans and some Lutherans also keep his day.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. the woman you're promised to is pregnant, and not by you. you could make it public. what do you do?
options: make it public so everyone knows it wasn't you.
end it quietly, to spare her shame.
fork.reveal: Matthew says he was minded to put her away privily, quietly, to spare her. then the angel came, and he took her as his wife.

original.note: Greek: a builder or craftsman, the word behind 'carpenter' in Matthew 13:55.

trapdoor: what you thought: the background figure in the nativity scene.
what it means: a just man who protected Mary, obeyed his dreams without a word, and is remembered as the carpenter who raised Jesus.
what a scholar hears: tektōn, a craftsman; and the Gospels record no words from Joseph at all — only what he did.
recall: mocked of the wise men, exceeding wroth

notes: 'The Gospels never record a word from Joseph': confirm (no direct speech of Joseph in Matthew or Luke).
'A missing twelve-year-old' comes from Luke 2:42 (cited text says 'twelve years old'); Luke 2:41–51 added to sources.
'Matthew says he arose and took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt' is said in KJV words (Matthew 2:14) without quotation marks; cited as paraphrase. Confirm or quote.
τέκτων meaning 'builder, craftsman' is a lexicon meaning (e.g. BDAG/LSJ), not an etymology; confirm.
Patronage (workers, fathers, families) attributed to Catholics 'in particular'; Orthodox/Protestant honoring kept soft. Confirm.
Engagement/betrothal and 'the law is on your side' (fork) simplify first-century marriage law; confirm acceptable.

Editor: Joseph is named again later (e.g. 'Joseph's son' in Luke 4:22), so 'isn't mentioned again' became 'never appears in a scene again'; cut 'teaches a trade' from the list of things the Gospels show him doing; 'the worst moment of his life' softened; the workshop upbringing is now tradition, resting on Mark 6:3 (added to sources).

Editor 2: Luke says Mary and Simeon 'said', not sang (hook fixed); Matthew first names Joseph in the genealogy, so 'introduces him' reworded; Matthew 13:54 says 'his own country', not Nazareth, so 'the town of Nazareth' became 'his home town'; 'whatever the tradition, the picture is the same' softened.
